newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Pressure mounts on Renault on closure.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Pressure mounts on Renault on closure.

text.p: Pressure mounted on French car maker Renault SA on Thursday to reconsider the closure of its Belgian factory as the European Commission blocked aid to a Spanish plant and workers began international protest action.
But Renault chairman Louis Schweitzer repeated that the decision to shut the assembly line at Vilvoorde, near Brussels, with the direct loss of 3,100 jobs, was "irrevocable".
It was a tough but necessary measure to ensure the ailing company met its objective of returning to breakeven this year, he told a news conference.

European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert, a Belgian Socialist, said earlier he had blocked Spanish government subsidies for a Renault plant in Valladolid, Spain, until the company changed its attitude on closing the Vilvoorde plant.

"It is of course absurd that they close a profitable company such as Vilvoorde and carry out additional investment in Spain with government aid," Van Miert told Belgian radio. EU officials said 500 million Belgian francs ($14.1 million) was at stake.
In Paris, trade union delegates stormed out of Renault's works council after management refused to allow a representative of the Belgian workforce to address the meeting.

Some 300 workers from Vilvoorde joined 600 French colleagues in a protest march at Renault's headquarters in the Paris suburb of Boulogne-Billancourt, chanting "same boss, same battle" and "Renault solidarity".
In addition to a one-hour work stoppage in France, Spain and Belgium on Friday, the unions called a demonstration in Paris next Tuesday when Renault has convened a European works council.
The announcement of the closure of the recently modernised plant in Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene's home town sparked anger in Belgium and France but initial enthusiasm on the Paris bourse.

Renault's share price shot up by nearly 20 percent last week after the restructuring plan was announced but it has slid back since Monday with dealers saying they feared political pressure could force the company to change its plans.
However the share finished the day up 0.43 percent at 139.80 francs on Thursday, compared with 130 francs before the restructuring plan.
Renault has also said it plans to cut more than 2,700 French jobs this year but a spokeswoman said the firm might transfer some of the affected Belgian workers to factories in France.
The smallest of Europe's six car manufacturers says it has no alternative to "downsizing" in the face of shrinking domestic demand, production overcapacity and a fierce price war.
Renault, which has 138,000 staff, is expected to announce a 1996 operating loss of up to three billion French francs ($520 million) on March 20, plus heavy charges for restructuring.
After Schweitzer refused to let him address the French works council, Belgian worker representative Raymond Smeulders read a defiant statement to a rally near company headquarters.
"Mr Schweitzer, the decision to close Vilvoorde is a cowardly, unproductive and uneconomical decision. I can assure you that we will fight till the end if we must," he declared.

"We are ready to discuss all possibilities of keeping the production site in Vilvoorde. Until then, we are going to keep our 'war chest', which is worth quite a lot," he said, referring to the stock of new cars which workers occupying the factory have said they have impounded.
French Prime Minister Alain Juppe, alarmed by the backlash in Belgium, summoned Schweitzer on Wednesday.
Without disputing the industrial logic of the closure, he urged Renault to open immediate talks with the Belgian workforce and authorities to cushion the human cost.

Schweitzer said in a statement on Thursday: "I want to meet a Belgian delegation as soon as possible. I regret the conditions did not make that possible this morning. I continue to make every effort so contact can be established."
South Korean car maker Kia Motors, meanwhile, denied a Belgian press report that it was considering buying the Vilvoorde plant. ($ = 35.34 Belgian Francs) ($ = 5.781 French Francs)
